title: Priming latency time-lapse journal — Cedric
body:
Quick goal: characterize how short, repeated bursts (10s windows) of traffic prime the KV/prefix caches and how latency evolves during the minutes after priming. This is a lightweight lab diary — rough timings, commands, and plots. Purpose is to decide whether to add short 'keepwarm' heartbeats in front of cold-path fallback for high-QPS customers.

Hypothesis summary:
- Small bursts will prime token-prefix caches quickly but may create a resonance where background eviction + new bursts re-trigger cold-paths after ~60–120s.
- The latency tail during that recovery is dominated by two things: (1) slow KV rebuilds with interleaved multiplexing stalls, (2) occasional GPU scheduler preemption during high co-tenancy.

Test harness (custom):
- bench-runner v0.3 (local dev cluster) on a 4x A100 pool (shared dev-fleet).
- Workload: 5k short prompts (avg tokens 64) issued as micro-bursts: 10s ON (poisson interarrival target qps=400), 50s OFF. Repeat 30 cycles.
- Concurrency: single client per pod, 16 async connections.
- Traces collected: p50/p95/p99 latency, kv-cache-hit-rate, gpu-preempt-events, epoll-wake counts.

Commands used:
- ./bench-runner --burst-interval 60s --burst-duration 10s --qps 400 --seq 64 --concurrency 16 --out priming-run-2025-11-02.log
- small script to sample observability API every 5s: scripts/sample-metrics.sh --series latency,p99,kv.hit,gpu.preempt --out samples.csv

Observed timeline notes (cycle-level):
- Cycle 1 (0–60s): immediate priming, p50 ~ 18ms, p95 52ms, p99 110ms, kv-hit: 82% after first ON window.
- Cycle 3 (~3 min): p99 shows intermittent spikes to 420–600ms for 3–6 requests clustered. These correlate with KV hit dips to ~38% for ~5–10s windows.
- Cycle 7–10 (7–17 min): steady degradation in kv-hit baseline between bursts (from 82% -> 45%). p95 drifts upward ~+40ms.
- Mid-run anomaly (~12:42:11): a GPU preempt event (node kernel) coincides with a 1.6s tail for ~8 requests. Node logs show ephemeral OOM-killer-like message but no container exit — looks like preemption/slow swapback.

Representative excerpt from samples.csv (time, p99_ms, kv_hit_pct):
2025-11-02T12:40:00Z,110,82
2025-11-02T12:41:00Z,125,78
2025-11-02T12:42:00Z,160,70
2025-11-02T12:43:00Z,600,38  # GPU preempt spike
2025-11-02T12:44:00Z,140,66

ASCII sparkline (p99 over first 20 minutes):
[0m]  110 120 130 160 600 140 150 170 200 220 190 210 430 180 160 150 140 170 200
normalized-sparkline: ▁▁▂▂▃█▂▂▃▃▂▃█▂▂▂▂▂▃▃

Observations and interpretation:
- Priming effect is quick (first ON window brings kv hit to >80%), but there is not a stable memory of primed prefixes: hit-rate decays within 50–90s depending on other tenant load. That suggests a small TTL on cache entries (eviction pressure) + aggressive LRU from multiplexed workloads.
- Tail spikes are two-pronged: the smaller spikes (100–300ms) map to cache-miss recomputation cost; the very large spikes (>500ms) are rare and map to platform-level events (GPU preempt or scheduler interference). Improving app-level priming won't eliminate the latter.
- Net effect on throughput-sensitive customers: if bursts reoccur within 30–40s, latency stays low. If bursts are spaced >60s, user-facing p95/p99 degrades noticeably.

Quick notes on mitigation options (pros/cons):
1) Keepwarm heartbeats (per-tenant short warm calls every 30s)
   - Pros: maintains kv-hit above 70–80% for many workloads, directly reduces p95
   - Cons: extra cost, scales with number of active tenants, adds ingress QPS and billing complexity
2) Smarter eviction tuning (increase per-tenant cache quota or tweak sampler)
   - Pros: no extra external traffic, solves root cause of TTL eviction
   - Cons: changes memory footprint; risk during multi-tenant spikes where we need headroom
3) Fast-path fallback optimization: reduce recompute time for cache misses (op-level improvements)
   - Pros: reduces small spikes without adding background traffic
   - Cons: requires runtime changes and careful microbench testing
4) Scheduled short warm windows (batched keepwarm for groups of tenants)
   - Pros: amortized cost, maintains efficiency at scale
   - Cons: more complex scheduling logic and potential jitter alignment issues

Mini-experiments (quick):
- Keepwarm 30s prototype (10 tenants): reduced p95 by ~28% and p99 by ~40% across runs, kv-hit stable at ~78%. CPU usage increased by ~6% on worker pods.
- Eviction-policy tweak (LRU aging factor -10%): improved steady kv-hit by ~9% but increased memory usage by ~12% and caused some fragmentation in dev cluster (need larger memory tests).

Actionable next steps (short list):
- Run a controlled 24h experiment with keepwarm-enabled for a bucket of non-sensitive tenants to validate cost scaling and collision with real irregular traffic patterns. -> Owner: Rosa Lin (block scheduled).
- Instrument better: add per-request tag for "priming-triggered" so we can separate recompute costs in traces. -> Owner: Cedric (this doc). PR: bench-scripts #87 (linked).
- Recreate GPU preempt scenario on a reserved node to see if pattern repeats under heavier baseline host load. -> Owner: Mateo.

Loose TODOs / notes to self:
- Probe whether eviction is purely LRU or has time-based TTL in the current KV codepath (check impl in runtime/cache/kv_store.cpp).
- Add a small synthetic that issues the same prefix repeatedly but with slightly different endings to test prefix granularity.
- Confirm billing implications of keepwarm: estimate ingress delta for 10k tenants at 30s heartbeats.

Closing remark: priming helps when bursts are frequent (<30–40s spacing). For customers with sparser bursts, keepwarm or smarter eviction is necessary. Platform incidents (GPU preempt) are orthogonal and need SRE-level fixes; they dominate the extreme p99 tails. This notebook is rough — will convert key findings to a short playbook draft once we validate 24h run.

End of entry.

Signature: Cedric M.
